title: Power and Water Cuts in Istanbul: How to See Them Coming, and What You Can Claim
excerpt: Where BEDAŞ, AYEDAŞ and İSKİ publish planned cuts, SMS alerts, the 186 and 185 lines, keeping your connection up, and what you can claim when a cut damages your laptop or runs past 10 hours.
bodyHtml:
Istanbul's power and water companies publish most planned cuts in advance. If you work from home, a minute spent checking can save a dead router in the middle of a call. This guide covers where to look, who to call, and what you can claim if a cut damages your equipment.

Who runs what

  • Electricity, European side: BEDAŞ (Boğaziçi Elektrik Dağıtım).

  • Electricity, Asian side: AYEDAŞ.

  • Water, the whole city: İSKİ (İstanbul Su ve Kanalizasyon İdaresi).

These are the distribution companies — the ones that do the work on the network and announce cuts. The company that sends your electricity bill can be a different one.

See planned cuts coming

BEDAŞ (European side)

  • The planned-cuts list is on the BEDAŞ website, and its outage map (kesinti.bedas.com.tr) shows planned and unplanned cuts.

  • You can sign up on the website for SMS alerts about planned cuts.

AYEDAŞ (Asian side)

  • The outage lookup on its Online İşlemler site shows current and planned cuts for an address.

  • The same information is on its WhatsApp line (0216 186 00 00), the Mobil 186 app and the 186 call center.

  • On request, AYEDAŞ sends an SMS 48 hours before a planned cut.

İSKİ (water)

  • The outage page on the İSKİ website lists water cuts by district and neighborhood.

  • The call center is 185 (0212 185 00 00 if you're calling from outside Istanbul).

When the power goes off

  1. Check whether it's just your apartment. If the hallway lights or the neighbors are out too, it's the building or the street.

  2. Look up your address on your side's outage page — the cut may already be listed.

  3. If it isn't listed, report it on 186 — the number for both BEDAŞ and AYEDAŞ. BEDAŞ's line answers 24/7.

Keep working through a cut

  • Your router goes down with the power, even if your laptop doesn't. A phone hotspot on a Turkish SIM is the simplest backup — see our SIM card and home internet guide.

  • The night before a planned cut, charge your laptop, phone and a power bank.

  • For a long cut, move: a café or a coworking session on the other side of the cut usually has power.

  • Before a planned water cut, fill a few bottles and a kettle.

If a cut damages your equipment

Under the national rules on electricity service quality, the distribution company has to compensate damage caused by its network — not damage caused by faulty wiring in your own home. As BEDAŞ and AYEDAŞ explain it:

  • Claim within 30 days of the damage, with the distribution company for your side (186, AYEDAŞ's WhatsApp line, or a customer service center).

  • Renters can claim. The claim belongs to the person using the electricity. If the account is in someone else's name, bring proof that you live there, such as your rental contract.

  • The company checks whether the damage came from its network. If it turns the claim down, it has to tell you why, with its technical report, within 10 working days.

  • What you'll need once a claim is accepted: the device's invoice (a copy is fine), a repair service's report, and an IBAN.

  • What you get: the company either has the device repaired (within 15 days) or pays your repair bill (within 5 working days of you handing in the invoice). If it can't be repaired, it pays the device's market value.

  • If you disagree, take it to a consumer arbitration committee or consumer court.

Keep invoices for your laptop, monitor and router somewhere you can find them — they're what makes a claim possible. The 30-day limit and the renter rule come from the regulation itself (Article 26), so if you're told otherwise, you can point to it.

Compensation for long cuts

Under the same regulation, the distribution company owes compensation to every affected user when:

  • a single cut lasts more than 10 hours in a city area, or

  • unannounced cuts in a calendar year go over the limits the regulator sets for how many and how long.

You don't have to apply — but you do have to tell them where to pay it. AYEDAŞ notifies users each month (with the bill, by SMS or by email) and pays to an IBAN in the user's name. BEDAŞ has a lookup on its website: enter the 10-digit service point number from your electricity bill and your ID or tax number.

A checklist for home workers

  • Know your side: BEDAŞ (European) or AYEDAŞ (Asian).

  • Sign up for planned-cut SMS alerts.

  • Have a Turkish SIM with data for a hotspot.

  • Keep a charged power bank.

  • Keep device invoices.

  • Save 186 (power) and 185 (water) in your phone.
